units.title: Me and you
units.goal: greet someone, say yes or no, and say please and thank you.

units.title: Who I am
units.goal: say your name and where you are from.

units.title: How and where I am
units.goal: ask how someone is, and say how and where you are.

units.title: What I want and have
units.goal: say what you want and what you have.

units.title: My people
units.goal: talk about the people in your life.

units.title: What people are like
units.goal: describe people and things: good, big, new, happy, tired.

units.title: Asking questions
units.goal: ask what, who, where, when, how and why.

units.title: When I don't understand
units.goal: say you don't understand or don't know, and say sorry.

units.title: Can you help me?
units.goal: ask for help politely and say what you can and need.

tips.title: Spanish drops "I" and "you"
tips.body: In Spanish, the verb's ending already tells you who is doing it. Soy means I am and eres means you are, so you don't need a separate word for I or you. To say I'm from Chile, just say soy de Chile. Add yo (I) or tú (you) only when you want to stress the person or compare two people, as in English when you say I am, but you are.

examples.es: Yo soy Luis y tú eres Ana.

tips.title: Two verbs for "to be"
tips.body: Spanish has two verbs that both mean to be: ser and estar. Use ser (soy, eres, es) for what someone is: their name, where they're from, their job, what they're like. Use estar (estoy, estás, está) for how someone is right now and where they are. So soy de México tells people where you come from, but estoy bien tells them how you feel today. If it's about how you feel or where you are at the moment, reach for estar.

examples.es: Soy Ana y estoy muy bien.
examples.en: I'm Ana and I'm very well.

examples.es: Él es de Chile y está aquí.
examples.en: He's from Chile and he's here.

tips.title: Verbs change with who does them
tips.body: A Spanish verb changes its ending to show who is doing it. Quiero means I want, quieres means you want, and quiere means he or she wants. Tener works the same way: tengo is I have, tienes is you have, and tiene is he or she has. Most of the time, an ending in -o means I, an ending in -s means you, and an ending in -e means he or she. Listen for the ending, because it tells you who, even when nobody says yo, tú or ella.

examples.es: Ella quiere un café y tiene mi café.
examples.en: She wants a coffee and has my coffee.

tips.title: Every noun is el or la
tips.body: In Spanish, every noun (a word for a person or a thing) is either masculine or feminine. Masculine words use el for the and un for a, like el hermano and un amigo. Feminine words use la for the and una for a, like la hermana and una amiga. This is true for things too, so coffee is masculine: el café. Words ending in -o are usually el and words ending in -a are usually la, but not always, so learn el or la together with each new word.

examples.es: Tengo un hermano y una hermana.
examples.en: I have a brother and a sister.

examples.es: La madre de Ana está aquí.

tips.title: Describing words come after and match
tips.body: In Spanish, a describing word usually comes after the thing it describes, so a big coffee is un café grande. It also matches that thing: use the -o ending for an el word and the -a ending for a la word, as in un amigo nuevo and una amiga nueva. When there is more than one, add -s to both words, as in dos amigos nuevos. Words that end in -e, like grande, are the same for el words and la words. So say the thing first, then make the describing word's ending match it.

examples.es: Mi hermana tiene una amiga nueva.
examples.en: My sister has a new friend.

tips.title: Questions and ¿ ¡
tips.body: In Spanish, a question opens with an upside-down ¿ and closes with ?, so you know from the start that it's a question. Exclamations work the same way, with ¡ at the start and ! at the end, as in ¡Hola! For a yes-or-no question, you can take a normal sentence and raise your voice at the end: eres de México means you are from Mexico, and ¿Eres de México? asks it. Question words always carry an accent mark, like qué, dónde and cómo. The accent doesn't change the sound much, but it marks the word as a question word, so keep it when you ask.

tips.title: No goes before the verb
tips.body: To say not in Spanish, you just put no right before the action word, the verb. So sé means I know, and no sé means I don't know. Spanish has no extra word like don't, so no entiendo means I don't understand. When you answer a question with no, you often say it twice: No, no sé means No, I don't know. The first no answers the question, and the second no goes before the verb.

tips.title: Tú and usted
tips.body: Spanish has two ways to say you. Use tú with friends, family and people your age, and usted to be polite with strangers and older people. With usted, the verb takes the same form as for he or she, so you say puede, not puedes. ¿Puedes ayudarme? asks a friend for help, and ¿Puede ayudarme? asks a stranger politely. If you're not sure which one to use, usted is the safe choice.

examples.en: Excuse me, can you help me?

tips.title: Going to: voy a…
tips.body: To talk about plans, Spanish uses ir a, just like going to in English. Take the right form of ir (voy, vas or va), add a, then add a second verb. That second verb stays in its basic form, the one ending in -ar, -er or -ir that you'd find in a dictionary, like hablar or entender. So voy a hablar means I'm going to speak, and ¿vas a venir? means are you going to come? Add hoy or mañana to say when your plan happens.

examples.en: Are you going to be home today?

examples.es: Mi amiga va a necesitar ayuda mañana.
examples.en: My friend is going to need help tomorrow.

tips.title: Regular -ar, -er and -ir verbs
tips.body: Most Spanish verbs follow one of three patterns, depending on whether they end in -ar, -er or -ir. To use one, drop that ending and add a new one that shows who is doing it. For I, add -o: hablo means I speak, como means I eat, vivo means I live. For you, add -as to -ar verbs and -es to the others: hablas, comes, vives. For he or she, add -a to -ar verbs and -e to the others: habla, come, vive.

tips.title: Gustar works backwards
tips.body: Spanish says I like backwards: me gusta el café really means the coffee pleases me. The thing you like does the pleasing, so the verb matches that thing, not you. Say me gusta for one thing and me gustan for two or more things. To ask someone if they like something, swap me for te: ¿te gusta el café? means do you like coffee?

tips.title: Me, te, lo go before the verb
tips.body: The small words for me, you, him, her and it are me, te, lo and la, and they go right before the verb. So I love you is te quiero, which word for word is you I love. Lo veo means I see him or I see it, and la veo means I see her. When the verb is in its dictionary form, the one ending in -ar, -er or -ir, the small word attaches to the end of it instead. So to help me is ayudarme, all one word.

examples.en: I love you so much, my love.

tips.title: Por and para
tips.body: Por and para can both mean for, but they point in different directions. Para looks ahead to a goal or to the person who gets something: para mi madre means for my mother, and para comer means in order to eat. Para can also give a deadline, so para mañana means by tomorrow. Por looks back at a reason or an exchange: you already know por favor, and gracias por todo means thanks for everything. Por can also mean through or around a place, so por aquí means around here.

examples.es: Este café es para mi madre.
examples.en: This coffee is for my mother.
Is there a bathroom around here?

tips.title: Talking about the past
tips.body: To talk about something that already happened, Spanish changes the end of the verb. For -ar verbs like hablar, drop the -ar and add -é for I or -ó for he or she, so hablé means I spoke and habló means he or she spoke. Say the accent clearly, because hablo with no accent means I speak, right now. Some very common verbs have their own short past forms, so learn them as words: tuve means I had, and hice means I did or I made. Fue has two meanings: it was, and he or she went, and the rest of the sentence tells you which one.

examples.es: Hablé con Ana y ella habló conmigo.
examples.en: I talked to Ana and she talked to me.

examples.es: Mi padre fue a la fiesta.
examples.en: My father went to the party.
I had a lot of work today.

cards.trick: NO is spelled and said like English no, so refusing in Spanish works just like in English.
SÍ sounds like see: when you see what someone means, you nod and say yes.
YO sounds like a rapper's "Yo!": that's me, I'm talking about myself.
ÉL sounds like the letter L: think of L for Lad, a he.

example.en: Do you want to go to the movies with me?

cards.trick: TÚ sounds like two: it takes two, me and you, to have a friendly chat.
ELLA sounds like Ella, a girl's name, and Ella is always a she.
GRACIAS sounds like gracious: a gracious person always says thank you.
HOLA sounds like "hello" with an O and an A: you holler hola to say hello.

example.en: Thanks, I won't insist. Goodbye, Ana!

cards.trick: ADIÓS sounds like "a dose": take a dose of courage before saying goodbye.
Por favor sounds like "for a favor", and that's what you're asking for when you say please.
Picture yourself proudly announcing I am soy sauce: yo soy.
cards.why: Use soy for who or what you are and where you're from; estoy for how or where you are right now.

cards.trick: DE sounds like day: you came FROM far away, a whole day's trip.
Eres sounds like heiress: you are an heiress.
cards.why: Use eres for who or what someone is; estás for how or where they are right now.

cards.trick: Es sounds just like the start of is: he es, she es.
cards.why: Use es for what someone or something is; está for how or where it is right now.

example.es: Yo soy Ana y él es Juan.

cards.trick: Y sounds like "ee": you squeal "eee!" when you get cake and ice cream.

example.es: Hola, soy Ana y soy de México.
example.en: Hi, I'm Ana and I'm from Mexico.

example.es: ¿Eres de México? Sí, soy de Monterrey.
example.en: Are you from Mexico? Yes, I'm from Monterrey.

cards.trick: De nada literally means "of nothing", like saying "it was nothing".

cards.hint: The everyday two-word way, literally "I call myself"
cards.trick: Llamo sounds a bit like "call me", and me llamo really means "I call myself".

cards.hint: informal; the everyday way, literally "how do you call yourself?"

example.en: Hi, what's your name? —My name is Ana.

cards.trick: It literally means "how do you call yourself?", where cómo is "how" and te llamas is "you call yourself".

cards.hint: The everyday two-word phrase, literally "much pleasure", that anyone can say, man or woman.

example.es: Hola, me llamo Ana. Mucho gusto.
example.en: Hi, my name is Ana. Nice to meet you.

cards.spain: Spain more often says encantado, or encantada if you are a woman.
cards.trick: Gusto means pleasure, like doing something with gusto, so mucho gusto is literally much pleasure.

cards.en: My name is Ana. Nice to meet you.
cards.hint: The everyday "I call myself" way, then the two-word phrase anyone can say, man or woman.

example.es: —Me llamo Ana. Mucho gusto. —Mucho gusto, Ana.
example.en: My name is Ana. Nice to meet you. Nice to meet you, Ana.

cards.spain: Me llamo Ana. Encantada. (Encantado or encantada is more common than mucho gusto in Spain.)

cards.why: Use estás for how or where someone is right now; eres for who or what they are.
Use está for how or where something is right now; es for what it is.

example.en: Ana is in Mexico, and you?

cards.trick: EN sounds like the start of 'inside': whatever is EN something is in it.

cards.hint: in a good way, also fine; not the filler well... (that is bueno)
cards.trick: BIEN sounds like "be in": when you're in good shape, you're doing well.
cards.why: Use bien for how someone is or how something is done; bueno describes what a person or thing is like.

cards.trick: Estoy sounds like "a stay": where I stay is where I am right now.
cards.why: Use estoy for how or where you are right now; soy for who or what you are.

example.es: Hola, Ana. Estoy aquí en México.
example.en: Hi, Ana. I'm here in Mexico.

cards.trick: AQUÍ sounds like a key: here is a key, right here in my hand.
MUY sounds like a cow's very loud MOO: that cow is very, very noisy.
MAL as in malfunction: a machine that malfunctions is working badly.
cards.why: Use mal for how you are or how something is done (estoy mal); malo describes a noun (un día malo).

example.es: Hola, Ana. Estoy muy bien, estoy aquí en México.
example.en: Hi, Ana. I'm very well, I'm here in Mexico.

cards.en: I'm very well, thank you. And you?

example.en: How are you? I'm very well, thank you. And you?

cards.trick: Word for word it means good days, plural, the way you would wish someone a good day.

example.es: Estoy en un hotel muy bueno.
example.en: I'm at a very good hotel.

cards.trick: UN sounds like oon, a short form of uno (one), so un libro is one book, a book.

example.en: I have a hotel in Mexico.

cards.trick: Tengo sounds like tango: I have a tango partner.

example.es: Ana tiene un hotel en México.
example.en: Ana has a hotel in Mexico.

cards.trick: MI sounds like me: anything that belongs to me is my stuff.
Quiero starts like query: you make a query when you want something.

example.en: Ana, do you want a chocolate?

cards.trick: TU sounds like "to you": the thing that belongs to you is yours.
cards.why: Without an accent, tu means your (tu casa); with an accent, tú means you (tú eres).

example.es: Sí, quiero un café, por favor.
example.en: Yes, I want a coffee, please.

cards.trick: CAFÉ sounds like the English café, where you go to drink coffee.

example.es: Buenos días, quiero un café, por favor.
example.en: Good morning, I want a coffee, please.

example.es: Hola, ¿tienes café? Quiero un café, por favor.
example.en: Hi, do you have coffee? I want a coffee, please.

cards.trick: EL sounds like the letter L, and L comes before M just like THE comes before a noun.
AMIGO sounds like "a meego": a friend who always says "me go too!"
HIJO sounds like "ee-ho": a son yells "ee-ho!" as he runs to his dad.
HIJA sounds like "ee-ha": a daughter shouts "yee-ha!" riding her pony.
PADRE sounds like padded chair: father's padded armchair that nobody else may sit in.
HERMANO sounds like "her man, oh": the guy always with her is just her brother.
HERMANA sounds like "her mama": your sister acts just like her mama, bossing you around.
MADRE sounds like "mad dray": your mother gets mad when you drag mud into the house.

cards.es: Tengo un hijo y una hija.
cards.en: I have a son and a daughter.

example.es: ¿Tienes hijos? Sí, tengo un hijo y una hija.
example.en: Do you have kids? Yes, I have a son and a daughter.

example.es: Ella es mi hermana y él es mi hermano.
example.en: She is my sister and he is my brother.

cards.en: I want to go, [but] I can't

example.es: Estoy bien, pero mi madre está mal.
example.en: I'm fine, but my mother isn't well.

cards.trick: PERO sounds like a pear-o: I wanted an apple, but I got a pear-o.

example.es: El café de aquí es muy bueno.
example.en: The coffee here is really good.

cards.trick: BUENO sounds like "bway-no": no way it's bad, it's good!
cards.why: Use bueno to describe a person or thing (good); use bien for how you are or how something is done (well).

example.es: Mi hermana también es muy buena.
example.en: My sister is also very good.

cards.trick: TAMBIÉN sounds like "Tom be in": whatever the plan, Tom wants to be in it too.
NUEVO sounds like "new-EH-vo": it even starts with "new".
PEQUEÑO sounds like peck-a-new: a tiny chick can only peck a new, small seed.

example.es: Mi hermana no es mala, es muy buena.
example.en: My sister isn't bad, she's very good.

cards.trick: MALO sounds like a moldy marshmallow: a bad treat nobody wants to eat.
cards.why: Use malo to describe a person or thing (una película mala); mal for how something goes or how you feel.

example.es: Mi padre es viejo, pero mi madre no.
example.en: My father is old, but my mother isn't.

cards.trick: VIEJO sounds like "Be a yo-yo": that toy is so old your grandpa played with it.
GRANDE sounds like grand: a grand piano is a really big piano.

example.es: Mi hermana está muy feliz aquí.
example.en: My sister is very happy here.

cards.trick: FELIZ sounds like Felix, the cat who is always happy and grinning.
CANSADO sounds like "can't sad-o": you're so tired you can't even manage to feel sad.

cards.es: Ella es una muy buena amiga.
cards.en: She is a very good friend.

example.es: ¿Ana? Sí, ella es una muy buena amiga.
example.en: Ana? Yes, she's a very good friend.

cards.hint: Said by a man; a woman says cansada.

example.en: How are you? —I'm tired but happy.

cards.trick: QUÉ sounds like "K?": a puzzled K-shaped question mark asking what.

cards.hint: neuter: an unnamed thing or idea, not este or esta

example.en: What is this? Is it coffee?

cards.trick: ESTO sounds like a stow: you point at a weird thing in the stowed box and ask, what is this?
CÓMO sounds like "come, oh?": you ask how someone will come over.

example.es: Estoy muy feliz porque mi hermana está aquí.
example.en: I'm very happy because my sister is here.

cards.trick: PORQUE sounds like "poor case": you lost the case because your lawyer was poor.
cards.why: Porque, one word with no accent, gives an answer (because); por qué, two words with an accent, asks why.

cards.trick: QUIÉN sounds like key-EN: someone knocks, and you ask who has the key.
DÓNDE sounds like "Don, they": where did Don and they go?

example.en: How much coffee do you want?

cards.trick: CUÁNTO sounds like quantity: when you ask how much or how many, you want the quantity.
cards.why: Use cuánto to ask how much or how many; cuándo, with a d, asks when.

cards.trick: CUÁL sounds like quail: three quails in a row, which one do you want?
cards.why: Use cuál to pick one from a set, as in ¿cuál es...?; use qué right before a noun or to ask what something is.

example.en: When do you want a coffee?

cards.trick: CUÁNDO sounds like "quand-oh?": you ask "oh, when?" with the accent like a raised eyebrow.
NO sounds just like English no: put it right before the verb to make anything a no, meaning not.

cards.hint: facts, information, how to do something

example.en: I don't know where it is.

cards.trick: Sé sounds like say: you can only say it if you know it.

cards.hint: facts, information, how to do something; informal

example.en: Do you know where Ana is?

cards.trick: Sabes sounds like savvy, and a savvy person knows things.

cards.hint: facts, information, how to do something

example.es: Mi madre sabe dónde está el café.
example.en: My mother knows where the coffee is.

cards.trick: English savvy comes from Spanish sabe, so someone savvy knows a lot.
HABLAR sounds like "blabber": people who blabber talk all day long.

cards.hint: the everyday word, as in "I don't get it" (not comprender)
cards.trick: ENTENDER sounds like "intend her": to understand what she intends, you have to listen to her.

example.es: Mi amiga es inglesa, de Londres.
example.en: My friend is English, from London.

cards.trick: INGLÉS sounds like "English" said quickly with a Spanish accent: in-GLÉS, in-GLISH.

cards.hint: apology or sympathy, not excuse me
cards.trick: Siento is like sentiment: lo siento literally means I feel it.
cards.why: Use lo siento for a real apology or sympathy; perdón for a quick sorry or to get past someone.

example.en: I'm sorry, I don't understand. Do you speak English?

cards.trick: Entiendo sounds like the entendre in double entendre, a phrase about two ways to understand something.

example.en: I don't understand. Do you speak English?
I don't understand. Can you repeat that, please?

cards.hint: object pronoun, attached to or before the verb
cards.trick: ME is spelled just like English me, so it's an easy one.

example.es: Lo siento, no te puedo entender.

example.en: Can you speak in English, please?

example.es: Mi hermana no puede hablar, está muy cansada.
example.en: My sister can't talk, she's very tired.

cards.trick: Puede sounds like pway-day, close to payday: on payday, he can buy anything.
NECESITAR sounds like necessity: when something is a necessity, you need it.
USTED sounds like "you steady": you speak steady and polite to a respected person.
cards.why: Use usted for strangers and older people; tú for friends, family and people your age.

example.en: My sister helps me a lot.

cards.trick: AYUDAR sounds like "I, you, dar": I give you a hand when you need help.
